title: Testing the decoy effect to improve online survey participation: Evidence from a field experiment

preliminary_study_findings.description: Respondents generally preferred close-ended questions over open-ended questions.
preliminary_study_findings.hypothesis: Open-ended questions would be perceived as less attractive than close-ended questions and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
preliminary_study_findings.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: close-ended questions 61.4% (n~129), open-ended questions 7.9% (n~17), indifferent 30.7% (n~64). Exact counts NOT PROVIDED in paper.

preliminary_study_findings.description: Most respondents indicated they would not participate if remuneration were received only after four weeks.
preliminary_study_findings.hypothesis: Delayed remuneration would be perceived as less attractive than sooner remuneration and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
preliminary_study_findings.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: Definitely not 1.0% (n~2), Probably not 85.1% (n~179), Probably yes 1.5% (n~3), Definitely yes 12.4% (n~26). Overall 86.1% would not respond if remuneration in four weeks.

main_study.study_name: Field experiment on the decoy effect in survey participation

findings.description: Randomization produced similar groups on most sociodemographic variables, except ethnicity.
findings.hypothesis: No explicit hypothesis; balance checks were used to compare control and decoy groups.

statistical_tests.claim: No age difference between control and decoy groups.
No gender difference between control and decoy groups.
Ethnicity differed between conditions; the decoy condition contained more White participants (67.7% vs 47.5%).
No religion difference between control and decoy groups at conventional significance levels.
No education difference between control and decoy groups.

findings.description: The presence of the decoy option increased completion of the target survey.
findings.hypothesis: Among those likely to take part in a survey, the presence of a decoy version of the same survey on the invitation will increase the chances of completing the target version.

raw_data.note: Table 2 / Table S3 reports decoy as 59.8%, but text, flow diagram, and participant-level data imply 57/102 = 55.9%

statistical_tests.claim: Target-survey completion was significantly higher in the decoy condition (55.9%) than in the control condition (32.7%).
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Results section 3.2.2 and Fig. 3

raw_data.note: As reported in Table 2, Model 1; Supplementary Table S3

statistical_tests.claim: In the unadjusted model, the decoy condition significantly increased the odds of completing the target survey relative to control.
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Table 2, Model 1; Supplementary Table S3

statistical_tests.claim: The decoy effect on target-survey completion remained statistically significant after adjustment for sociodemographic variables.
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Table 2, Model 1; Supplementary Table S3

findings.description: A strong order effect was observed within the decoy condition: the decoy increased participation only when the target survey was presented first.
findings.hypothesis: Presentation order may influence the decoy effect because responses can favor options appearing earlier in a list.

statistical_tests.model: Model 2 - unadjusted, target first vs control
statistical_tests.claim: Showing the target first greatly increased target-survey completion (82.7%) relative to control (32.7%).
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Table 2, Model 2; Supplementary Table S4

statistical_tests.model: Model 2 - adjusted, target first vs control
statistical_tests.claim: The target-first order effect remained large and significant after adjustment for sociodemographics.
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Table 2, Model 2; Supplementary Table S4

statistical_tests.model: Model 2 - unadjusted, decoy first vs control
statistical_tests.claim: There was no evidence that showing the decoy first increased target-survey completion (28.0%) relative to control (32.7%).
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Table 2, Model 2; Supplementary Table S4

statistical_tests.model: Model 2 - adjusted, decoy first vs control
statistical_tests.claim: There was no decoy effect when the decoy was shown before the target, even after adjustment.
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Results section 3.2.2 and Table 2; Supplementary Table S4

findings.description: Most target-survey completers in the decoy condition reported that the decoy had at least somewhat influenced their decision to participate.
findings.hypothesis: The decoy option should be perceived as influencing participation decisions.
findings.raw_outcomes: Among the 57 individuals in the decoy condition who completed the target survey, 33/57 (57.9%) at least somewhat agreed that the decoy survey had influenced their decision to participate.

findings.description: There was little evidence for adverse question-response behavior or non-response bias, except for ethnicity differences.
findings.hypothesis: The decoy should increase participation without negatively influencing question response behavior or inducing substantial non-response bias.

statistical_tests.claim: Among target-survey completers, ethnicity differed between conditions: more White participants in the decoy condition (70.2% vs 36.4%).
statistical_tests.location: Main paper section 3.2.3; Supplementary Table S5

statistical_tests.claim: No age difference among target completers across conditions.
No gender difference among target completers across conditions.
No religion difference among target completers across conditions.
No education difference among target completers across conditions.

statistical_tests.variable: FCQ total score (8-40) among target completers

raw_data.note: Exact group means and SDs NOT PROVIDED

statistical_tests.claim: There was no statistically significant difference in FCQ score distributions across the two experimental conditions.
statistical_tests.location: Main paper section 3.2.3; Supplementary Fig. S4

statistical_tests.claim: No age difference between completers and non-completers.
No gender difference between completers and non-completers.
No overall ethnicity difference between completers and non-completers.
No religion difference between completers and non-completers.
No education difference between completers and non-completers.
